resident.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old man presented with neck pain of 6 months' duration, with paraesthesia radiating from both shoulders to the fingers, and worsening weakness in both lower extremities over 5 months.
resident.history: The patient had intermittent neck pain with paraesthesia in both shoulders radiating to the fingers, mostly during activities, for 6 months. There was no prior trauma. Over the following 5 months, the pain and paraesthesia worsened, and he developed weakness in both lower extremities. He consulted a neurosurgeon, who stated there was nerve entrapment. He underwent physiotherapy for 4 months without improvement. He then presented to our hospital. He worked as a contractor and mostly sat behind a desk. He denied any decrease in body weight or appetite and had no history of chronic cough.
resident.physical_exam: On physical examination, general condition was unremarkable (further details not documented). There was no tenderness on palpation along the midline. Examination of the cervical spine showed positive Lhermitte test, finger-escape test, grip-and-release test, Hoffman-Tromner sign, and Spurling sign. The patient was able to move his neck normally. Further examination revealed diminished motoric strength in all extremities with positive Babinski reflex and clonus, with normal patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes. He had urinary retention and faecal incontinence. Radiographic examination showed straight cervical spine with mid-sagittal diameter of 10 mm and a Torg ratio of 0.37. There was osteophyte, endplate irregularity, and disc-space narrowing at C4-C5 levels with spur formation at C3 through C5. Magnetic resonance imaging showed cervical canal stenosis at C4-C5 levels and spinal cord compression. Laboratory findings were unremarkable except for leukocytosis.

Radiographic straight cervical spine with mid-sagittal diameter 10 mm and Torg ratio 0.37
Osteophyte, endplate irregularity, and disc-space narrowing at C4-C5 with spur formation at C3-C5
MRI cervical canal stenosis at C4-C5 with spinal cord compression

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord at C4-C5 with compressive myelopathy, plus a likely cervical radiculopathy (C5 or C6) suggested by radicular symptoms and a positive Spurling sign.

red_flags.finding: Positive Spurling sign with paresthesias radiating from shoulders to fingers
red_flags.rationale: Indicates a radicular component in addition to myelopathy. The MRI report describes canal stenosis and cord compression but does not mention foraminal stenosis; if present, decompression should address the nerve roots as well.

red_flags.finding: Normal patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes despite positive Babinski reflex and clonus
red_flags.rationale: Upper motor neuron lesions typically cause hyperreflexia. Normal DTRs may reflect early myelopathy or a coexisting peripheral neuropathy, but they do not undermine the evidence of cord compression.
Not explained by cervical stenosis and not an alternative cause of the myelopathy. It may indicate an unrelated infection or inflammation but does not alter the localization or indication.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The MRI report describes central canal stenosis and cord compression at C4-C5, which explains the myelopathic syndrome. However, the radicular symptoms (shoulder-to-finger paresthesias, positive Spurling sign) are not directly explained by the reported imaging; foraminal stenosis is not described.

(3) Leukocytosis—coexisting—incidental laboratory abnormality not explained by cervical stenosis and not an alternative cause of cord compression.

physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge the progressive myelopathy and the evidence that delay may risk irreversible cord damage. However, the patient is only 50 years old and has not had a structured, supervised conservative program with clear goals and close monitoring. I propose a formal 3-6 month course of intensive physical therapy, core strengthening, posture management, and symptom control, with defined failure criteria. Success rates from structured conservative care in mild-to-moderate compressive myelopathy are around 30%, but in this case with severe myelopathy and already failed physiotherapy, that figure may be optimistic. Nevertheless, given the risks of surgery, a time-limited trial under strict supervision is a reasonable first step. If there is no improvement after 6 weeks or if neurological deficits worsen, I would accept surgery.

vice_opinions.assessment: This record is most consistent with severe, progressive C4-5 degenerative cervical myelopathy with probable concomitant cervical radiculopathy. Bilateral limb weakness, pathological long-tract signs, loss of hand dexterity, and sphincter dysfunction indicate advanced cord dysfunction rather than a pain-predominant or mild stable syndrome. The reported canal dimensions and MRI correlation support clinically significant compression; failure of four months of physiotherapy further weakens the case for additional non-operative treatment. A further 3–6 month conservative trial risks additional, potentially irreversible neurological deterioration, particularly bladder/bowel and gait/limb function. Before any intervention, the unexplained leukocytosis should be repeated and assessed for infection or other systemic cause, and imaging must be reviewed or repeated to define levels, sagittal alignment, foraminal disease, compression morphology, and cord signal change. The current imaging description is insufficient to select a defensible anterior versus posterior operation with confidence.
proposed_options: Proceed on an urgent elective basis with surgical decompression after prompt updated/reviewed MRI (including foraminal assessment and cord T2 signal), dynamic cervical radiographs, and perioperative investigation of leukocytosis; choose the approach once compression morphology, alignment, and number of clinically relevant levels are verified.

If pathology is principally ventral and confined to C4-5, with relevant C3-5 anterior osteophyte/disc disease and acceptable alignment, consider anterior cervical decompression and fusion at the confirmed level(s), with foraminal decompression as indicated.

If review demonstrates multilevel stenosis, posteriorly amenable compression, and preserved lordosis, consider a posterior decompression strategy, with fusion if instability, deformity, or the extent of bony resection makes this necessary.

Use only a very short, closely monitored non-operative interval if the director judges that diagnostic or medical clarification is required; it should not be framed as a 3–6 month rehabilitation trial. Any worsening weakness, gait, dexterity, or sphincter function should trigger immediate surgical reassessment.
disagreement_points: I would question the defensibility of a planned 3–6 month conservative programme in a patient already reporting progressive quadriparetic features and urinary retention/faecal incontinence. The cited conservative-care experience is not readily transferable to this severity of myelopathy.

The exact operative approach cannot responsibly be fixed from the present record because the MRI lacks description of cord signal, foraminal stenosis, direction of compression, and full-level disease, while sagittal alignment beyond straightening is incompletely characterized.

Leukocytosis is not explained by degenerative stenosis and should not be disregarded before instrumentation or fusion, although it should not automatically become a reason for prolonged neurological delay if infection is excluded.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you consider the sphincter dysfunction and progressive bilateral weakness sufficient to designate this as urgent decompression once medical clearance and imaging review are completed?
Would you direct repeat MRI/CT and dynamic radiographs before listing, or accept expedited formal review of the existing studies if they can be obtained immediately?

Given the incomplete morphology data, do you wish the operative plan to remain conditional—anterior decompression/fusion for focal ventral C4-5 disease versus posterior decompression for confirmed multilevel, lordotic disease?
What threshold for leukocytosis work-up and anaesthetic airway assessment would you require before proceeding, balancing infection risk against risk of further cord injury?
vice_opinions.public_message: The dominant concern is progressive, severe cervical myelopathy with sphincter involvement and concordant C4-5 cord compression after unsuccessful physiotherapy. In my view, this warrants expedited clarification for decompression rather than a routine additional 3–6 month rehabilitation course, but the final urgency and approach should follow your judgement after the actual imaging, leukocytosis, airway status, alignment, and foraminal involvement are verified.

director_rulings.final_decision: The meeting is closed on expedited preoperative clarification before a final operative listing. Surgery is indicated on the current record because of progressive cervical myelopathy with bilateral weakness and sphincter dysfunction, but operation will proceed only after the stated imaging, infection, and airway issues are resolved and the patient/family complete a detailed decision meeting.
delegated_tasks: Radiologist: urgently obtain and formally review the original cervical MRI; if it is unavailable or inadequate, characterize compression direction, cord T2 signal, foraminal stenosis, and all involved levels on repeat MRI.

Resident: repeat CBC with differential and obtain an expedited clinical evaluation for the source of leukocytosis; escalate cultures and infection assessment if fever, focal infectious symptoms, or persistent/unexplained leukocytosis are present.

Anesthesiologist: perform a documented airway assessment and perioperative review, including feasibility of the required positioning and a plan to maintain spinal-cord perfusion with a MAP target of at least 85 mmHg.
Neurologist: document a baseline serial neurological examination, including motor function, gait if safe, and bladder/bowel status, and identify any deterioration requiring urgent escalation.
Physiatrist: provide only monitored supportive rehabilitation and safety measures during the short workup interval; do not institute a prolonged conservative trial in place of decompression planning.
Vice_director: review the completed imaging and clearance results with the surgical team and confirm the lowest-risk decompression approach and contingency arrangements before listing.
director_rulings.reason_for_delay: The current record does not adequately define compression morphology, foraminal involvement, cord signal, full-level disease, airway risk, or the cause and perioperative significance of leukocytosis; these issues must be clarified without allowing a routine months-long conservative delay in a patient with progressive deficits and sphincter dysfunction.

director_rulings.public_message: The patient has a strong present indication for decompression: progressive bilateral myelopathic weakness, pathological long-tract signs, sphincter dysfunction, concordant C4-5 cord compression, and failure of prior physiotherapy. I reject a routine 3-6 month conservative programme. Nevertheless, in view of the unreviewed/incomplete MRI morphology, unexplained leukocytosis, and undocumented airway assessment, I will not fix an approach or list for instrumentation today. We will complete an expedited workup and reconvene for operative approval; confirmation of significant compressive C4-5 disease without active infection or prohibitive anaesthetic risk will lead to surgery. The least-risk approach will remain conditional: focal ventral C4-5 disease may favor anterior decompression and fusion, while confirmed multilevel disease with suitable alignment may require an alternative decompression strategy. If infection is identified, or if anaesthetic assessment identifies a prohibitive risk, surgery will be paused for urgent treatment and reassessment; if neurological function or sphincter control worsens during workup, the team must escalate urgently rather than wait for a rehabilitation trial.
